newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mark/yen reserves $35.3 bln at Q3 end.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mark/yen reserves $35.3 bln at Q3 end.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York said on Thursday that U.S. reserves of marks and yen totalled $35.3 billion at the end of the third quarter versus $35.6 billion on June 30.

"At the end of the quarter, the foreign currency reserve holdings of the Federal Reserve System and the (Treasury's) Exchange Stabilization Fund (ESF) were valued at $19.4 billion and $15.9 billion, respectively, and consisted of German mark and Japanese yen," the New York Fed said in the quarterly report on Treasury and Federal Reserve Foreign exchange Operations.
The report showed mark and yen reserves totalled $35.6 billion at the end of the second quarter.
The data showed the Fed held $13.0 billion in marks at the end of the third quarter while Treasury's ESF mark reserves stood at $6.6 billion.
Also, the Fed held $6.4 billion in yen reserves while the ESF's yen reserves stood at $9.3 billion.
Peter Fisher, New York Fed executive vice president and manager for the system open-market account for the Federal Open Market Committee, prepared the report which is presented in Congress.

Fisher noted the dollar was mostly stable during the third quarter, rising 1.6 percent against the yen, 0.1 percent versus the mark and also 0.1 percent on a trade-weighted basis against the currencies of the Group of Ten leading industrial countries.
"Over the quarter, the dollar was supported by expectations the Federal Reserve would tighten monetary policy, in contrast to expectations for steady policy in German and Japan," the report said.

"In addition, sentiment for the prospect of broad participation in the European Monetary Union shifted from doubt early in the quarter to growing confidence late in the quarter, lending support to the dollar against the mark," the report also said.
Fisher noted U.S. monetary authorities did not intervene in the foreign exchange market in the July-September period, making it the fourth consecutive quarter without currency intervention.
Fisher said the four-quarter stretch was "the longest period without intervention since April 1981-June 1982."

Fisher also attributed the stability of the dollar in the third quarter to the fact "the U.S. economic performance has been awfully good" -- to the point the "foreign exchange market is surprised" that dollar-negative scenarios did not materialize.
